title: Vishal Bhardwaj Sets ‘Rashomon’-Style Film on Tarun Tejpal Rape Case After Bombay High Court Conviction (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Indian auteur Vishal Bhardwaj is developing a film based on the Tarun Tejpal rape case, the director confirmed with Variety, hours after the Bombay
body:
Indian auteur Vishal Bhardwaj is developing a film based on the Tarun Tejpal rape case, the director confirmed with Variety, hours after the Bombay High Court overturned a Goa sessions court acquittal and convicted the former Tehelka editor of rape, sentencing him to 10 years’ rigorous imprisonment.

	Bhardwaj, whose adaptations of Shakespeare – “Maqbool,” “Omkara,” “Haider” – have established him as one of Hindi cinema’s foremost interpreters of moral complexity, said he has read the Goa trial court’s 527-page judgment multiple times and described the divergence between the two rulings as the creative catalyst. He was in Goa for the hearing of the case.
	

	“The contradiction between the two judgments makes it a perfect case for a ‘Rashomon’-style narrative,” Bhardwaj tells Variety. “There are a lot of facts and incidents in this case that nobody knows about, and people will be amused and surprised to discover them on screen.”


	He said the density of the legal record is precisely what drew him in.

	“As they say, the devil lies in the detail,” Bhardwaj says. “How do you expect people to go through the tiring, dry legal language of a 500-plus-page court judgment? I have gone through the minutest details. I have read the judgment many times and am still grappling with it. It’s a very important case for society.”

	Bhardwaj was careful to stress that his approach has not yet hardened into a fixed point of view. “It’s too early for me to make up my mind on what the film is about,” he says, “but I’m very clear that the approach must be that of a dispassionate observer, like a true film journalist, if I may say so.”
	

	That neutrality, he added, is structural as much as ethical. “Any crime of this nature, one with many points of view beyond reasonable doubt, must be approached without preconceived ideas or a biased starting point,” he says. “No story is complete without all the different points of view, especially in a “Rashomon” structure, because half a glass of water is also half empty at the same time – the only difference is perspective.”

	On casting, Bhardwaj set an unusual brief. “I want the actor to be unaware of the crime, if possible, and to set the judgments aside,” Bhardwaj says. “I would love for him to approach it as fiction.”

	The project is being produced by Bhardwaj alongside a major Bollywood studio, which he declined to name. He deflects a question about his authority on Shakespeare with characteristic self-deprecation. “I’m blessed by the almighty himself, otherwise how could an average student from a small town become an authority on Shakespearean adaptations?”

	He was equally expansive on what the film ultimately represents. “It’s not about India in 2026,” he says. “It’s about the truth, which must come out at any cost, at any 26th year of any century.”

	The Tejpal case has had one of the longest legal arcs in recent Indian criminal history. The former editor was arrested in 2013 after a junior colleague accused him of sexual assault. A Goa sessions court acquitted him in 2021, a verdict the state challenged. The Bombay High Court’s ruling on Aug. 6 called the trial court judgment “perverse” and relied on the complainant’s testimony, CCTV footage, and Tejpal’s own apology emails as evidence of guilt. Tejpal has said he will appeal to the Supreme Court.

schema.headline: Vishal Bhardwaj Sets ‘Rashomon’-Style Film on Tarun Tejpal Rape Case After Bombay High Court Conviction (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Thomas Heise’s Final Documentary ‘Übergang,’ a Potential Locarno Highlight, Reflects on Time and Transience
description: Thomas Heise‘s final film, “Übergang,” arrives at the Locarno Film Festival as both a portrait of one of Germany’s most influential documentary film
body:
Thomas Heise‘s final film, “Übergang,” arrives at the Locarno Film Festival as both a portrait of one of Germany’s most influential documentary filmmakers and the completion of a project left unfinished by his death. 

	Premiering in the festival’s out of competition section, the film traces Heise’s life through newly shot footage, archival material and photographs, sewing together a meditation on time and transition.


	Heise, whose body of work chronicled the lives of ordinary people across East Germany during reunification and the decades that followed, began developing “Übergang” as a portrait of Berlin’s Schönhauser Allee before his death in 2024. Longtime collaborators Peter Badel and Chris Wright ultimately completed the documentary, shaping a film that explores the filmmaker’s life and enduring relationship with German history.
	

	Produced by Ma.ja.de. Filmproduktion, “Übergang” at once imports you to Schönhauser Allee through patient, black and white street-level scenes of normal life: commuters boarding a tram, quiet revelers at a carnival, a couple in conversation. Voice over paints the picture of the man behind the camera, and through carefully placed interview vignettes of Heise, the observer becomes the observed. “Übergang” draws together contemporary observations set against Heise’s experiences growing up in East Berlin to shed light on the political and social transformations that defined both his life and art.

	Variety spoke with co-directors Peter Badel and Chris Wright ahead of the film’s world premiere at Locarno.

	The title “Übergang” suggests a transition or a passage. When did this emerge as the central theme of the film?
	

	Peter Badel: Here we are referring to a draft text that Thomas Heise wrote during the preparatory phase of the project. He was drawn to the dual meaning of the term “Übergang.” The film is largely shot around the station on Berlin’s Schönhauser Allee, a busy interchange between public transport lines, but the title also hints at the idea of change in society. Our film covers the period of transition from East Germany to the fall of the Wall and beyond. That includes the current climate of war and rearmament, and the shift away from the traditional politics of the left and right toward a direction that seeks to make us forget the lessons learned from two world wars and a Europe destroyed by the Nazis. For Chris and me, there was never any other title for the film than the one Thomas had chosen. 

	Was it difficult to preserve Thomas’s artistic voice and vision while creating a new work after his death?

	Chris Wright: Thomas wanted work on the film to continue unchanged after his death. But of course, that was an impossible task, because his death changed everything. We decided it was vital that it become our own film, and that we make our own decisions about how to shape it. But at the same time, everyone working on the film had a long history of collaborating with Thomas. For me personally, that meant I could often almost hear his voice in the edit, saying, “Let’s try a scene like this. Let’s put that in. Let’s leave that out.” His aesthetic had become almost second nature.

	Badel: Another big factor was Thomas’ personal archive, which his husband Michael gave us full access to. Going through all that material, Thomas remained a critical and productive partner for us even after his sudden death. Of course, we missed his proven ability to cut things and, in doing so, amplify the fragmentary nature of his work. But I believe we remained true to his playful spirit.

	How did you bring the various elements of the film (new footage, archival material, photos and text) together into a single narrative?

	Badel: First we explored approaches that proved to be dead ends. I shot lots of interviews with friends and collaborators, for example. We also tried to incorporate too many aspects of Thomas’ work. Then Chris had the idea to take a break and go through all the original archive recordings of Thomas we could find to see how they worked cinematically.
	

	Wright: I wanted the film to incorporate as much unseen, or hardly seen, material as possible. So there are lots of outtakes (particularly from Thomas’ last film, “Heimat is a Space in Time”), VHS footage we found on tapes and hard drives, diary excerpts, unpublished texts and archive interviews. As much of the film as possible is told through new combinations of his own words and images. The fragmentary montage remains true to his approach. We don’t explain exactly where the materials come from. What is important is the dialogue they enter into with each other. At the same time, it was vital not to make a homage or an anecdotal work. We wanted the film to take a similar approach to Thomas as a character as “Heimat” took toward his own family. We tell a story of lived history, the way the emotions and experiences of a life can be shaped by the politics and society it takes place in.



	

									Courtesy of Peter Badel, Chris Wright
	



	The film’s final scene condenses a great deal of meaning into a single moment. Can you describe how you came across this interview and this quote?

	Badel: During the many days of filming at Schönhauser Allee station, we frequently encountered Michael, whom we observed (sometimes up close, sometimes from a greater distance among all the passers-by) as he waited for spare change at his spot by the subway stairs. We talked with him about the social divide around the station and discovered that he knew Thomas Heise by sight. He had also heard about Thomas’ death.

	Wright: Time and transience were two of Thomas’ biggest concerns in his filmmaking. And here, it is this homeless man, begging for change, who names them. Thomas often put unnoticed lives at the center of his films. So it only seemed fitting that Michael should have the last words in this film about Thomas.

	What do you hope the audience will learn about Thomas Heise through “Übergang?”

	Badel: I would be very pleased if Thomas’ remark about this film: “The author is a character in the film,” has become tangible and vivid through our work. And I hope that even people who don’t know much about him will find his fascinating way of thinking about and presenting time inspiring.

	Wright: I think that, with Thomas, we’ve lost an important critical voice for our times. I hope the film will remind people that it’s vital to keep questioning the status quo. Otherwise, as Thomas says, things can easily change for the worse, and you won’t notice until it’s too late.

schema.headline: Thomas Heise’s Final Documentary ‘Übergang,’ a Potential Locarno Highlight, Reflects on Time and Transience

title: Ricky Gervais’ Netflix Animated Comedy ‘Alley Cats’ Is Surprisingly Bittersweet: TV Review
description: To kick off the third episode of the Netflix animated comedy “Alley Cats,” protagonist Gus — an overweight orange tabby voiced by writer, creator an
body:
To kick off the third episode of the Netflix animated comedy “Alley Cats,” protagonist Gus — an overweight orange tabby voiced by writer, creator and frequent director Ricky Gervais (think Garfield with a distinctly working class British accent) — describes his plan for the day. It starts with an achievable goal. Then: “Get distracted immediately. Do loads of weird, pointless shit that somehow makes stuff worse. Kill something. Eat bits of it. Give up our mission. Come home here. Sleep for 14 hours.”
	

	“Home,” in this case, is a derelict London rowhouse where Gus and his mates Puke (David Earl), Fang (Andrew Brooke) and Olive (Diane Morgan, better known as daft presenter Philomena Cunk) have taken to squatting. There, the cats watch TV, from a “Love Island” knockoff called “Thick and Single” to news footage of looting to nature documentaries, chat about nothing and generally do as Gus describes. “Alley Cats” ambles along as such for half a dozen sub-20-minute chapters — though the show is tinged throughout with a melancholy that’s a little surprising from the typically acerbic Gervais.


	Given the other series’ swift cancellation, it’s unlikely many viewers will have watched both “Alley Cats” and “Kevin,” the Amazon Prime Video series with a similar premise co-created by Aubrey Plaza. But comparing the two, as is inevitable for a critic commissioned to review each in turn, proves instructive. Both are cartoons for adults distributed via streaming, centered on feline protagonists in major cities. Yet “Kevin” is louder, wackier and more joke-dense — one might even say more American — than “Alley Cats,” which is more downbeat and droll by comparison. 
	

	“Alley Cats” also organizes itself around social caste, as befits its country of origin. The titular crew also hang around with a housecat they nickname Ponce (Tom Basden), who’s more genteel in every sense of the term than his friends. He sounds posh; he’s spoiled with pudding; he’s neutered and thus immune to baser urges, including Olive’s unrequited crush. The rest of the crew are more base, volleying the c-word — rhymes with “runt” — around freely as they debate useless topics like whether four cats could take down “one fat kid” or if bees are edible. (Most laughs come from these mumbled, mundane exchanges rather than conventional setups and punchlines.) Puke, the mangiest of the group, admits his private parts are “smashed up” because “I gave a hedgehog anal.” 

	But “Alley Cats” doesn’t just revel in the nastiness of feral life. The show also depicts its hardships with disarming frankness, even verging on despondency. An associate of the crew is introduced and then fatally run over in seconds. A deadbeat dad is reassured that, since his kittens were adopted and grew into well-adjusted triplets, “maybe you not being around was their best chance.” The last line of the season — not really a spoiler, since there’s not much context necessary — is “we’re all gonna die soon.” Sometimes, this undercurrent of gloom tips over into outright nihilism. (“Fuck people,” Gus proclaims in one of his many rants at the television. “I can’t wait for people to wipe people off the face of the Earth.”) More often, though, the mood is more one of resignation to a hardscrabble existence that also has its pleasures. 

	The serialized plot of “Alley Cats” comes from a lost kitten (Jo Hartley) the strays resolve to help find her way back home. Gervais isn’t overtly sentimental in depicting Gus’ growing affection for his young, quite cutely drawn (her eyes are enormous) young charge; in fact, the story resolves on a fittingly bittersweet note for the overall tone. But there is a real tenderness that’s thrown into the mix with the lewd banter and glass-half-empty outlook. “Alley Cats” is so compressed that it ends up stopping short of real heft. A subplot about Gus’ ailing mother is introduced so hastily it almost bewilders; on a broader level, this is fundamentally a hangout sitcom about free-range felines. The show nonetheless takes an unexpected direction that makes for an enjoyably low-key binge. Even bullshitting cats have feelings.
	

	All six episodes of “Alley Cats” are now streaming on Netflix.

schema.headline: Ricky Gervais’ Netflix Animated Comedy ‘Alley Cats’ Is Surprisingly Bittersweet: TV Review

title: Locarno Open Doors Buzz Title ‘Chapa 100,’ From Ique Langa, Adds Luminalia, Mo Harare, Mostafa El Kasha (EXCLUSIVE)
description: “Chapa 100,” the 2025 Atlas Workshops Development Award winner, now a potential highlight at Locarno’s Africa-focused strand Open Doors, has been bo
body:
“Chapa 100,” the 2025 Atlas Workshops Development Award winner, now a potential highlight at Locarno’s Africa-focused strand Open Doors, has been boarded by Italy-based sales agent Luminalia.

	Written and directed by Mozambique’s Ique Langa, “Chapa 100” has also added as an associate producer Mo Harawe, whose “The Village Next to Paradise” screened in Cannes Festival’s 2024 Un Certain Regard to enthusiastic reviews, Variety hailing it as a “quietly powerful film.”
	

	Also on board are Egyptian cinematographer Mostafa El Kashef, and a third production partner, Mozambique’s Better Films – signs of a building production in which talent and industry wants in. 


	Also penned by Langa, “Chapa 100” marks the filmmaker’s follow-up to feature debut “The Prophet” (“O Profeta”), which world premiered in main competition this year at the IFF Rotterdam and now forms part of Locarno’s Open Doors Screenings. 

	In advanced development, “Chapa 100” is lead produced by filmmaker Lara Sousa at Kulunga Filmes, based out of Mozambique capital Maputo, behind “Nós, Povo das Ilhas,” directed by Elson Santos and Sousa. Pedro Borges at Portugal’s Midas Filmes, a past Kulunga partner, co-produces. 

	Shot with an observational style, priming social realism and emotional insight, “Chapo 100” lifts off into a magical realist style which, along the lines of Gabriel García Márquez’s “One Hundred Years of Solitude,” says much about the collective mindset and heart of Maputo dwellers and the illusions of individual characters, “celebrating the resilience, tenderness, and humanity found in the city’s everyday rhythms,” Langa and Sousa said in a statement. 
	

	In it, Sitoé, an 80-year-old flower vendor meets Valentina, a vegetable seller in her seventies. A simple flower sparks a quiet romance. When a thief steals Valentina’s rented wig, Sitóe runs after him and is struck dead by a speeding chapa, a local minibus. His spirit becomes tied to the vehicle that killed him, however, and flowers begin to bloom within it.

	“‘Chapa 100’ is my love letter to Maputo. I wanted to portray the city not simply through its streets, but through the people who give it its heartbeat. By bringing together professional actors and non-professional performers from the city itself, the film seeks to capture something truthful and deeply human,” Langa told Variety. 

	“Blending realism with magical poetry, ‘Chapa 100’ is ultimately a story about love, memory, and the invisible bonds that connect us and to the places we call home,” he adds.

	Langa has completed a seven-week residency at MacDowell, where, he told Variety, he had the “opportunity to deepen the screenplay and refine the emotional core of the story.” 

	“Chapa 100” recently received the Cultiv’Art / Expertise France Development Grant, one of the largest international development grants ever awarded to a Mozambican feature film project. Together with the Atlas Workshop Development Prize, this marks an important step in the film’s international journey, noted Luminalia’s head of sales and festivals, Tommaso Priante.

	In a drive into sub-Saharan African cinema, Luminalia is also representing “The Prophet” and “Atcha Atcha,” the new doc by award winning Senegalese director Mamadou Dia.

	Dia’s debut, “Nafi’s Father,” won the award for best first feature at the 2019 Locarno Film Festival as well as the Golden Leopard in its Filmmakers of the Present section.

	Screening out of competition at this year’s Locarno Festival, “Atcha, Atcha” follows students in their third and final year at the École des Sables, founded by legendary Senegalese dancer and choreographer Germaine Acogny and described by Dia as “the Ivy League of dance schools in sub-Saharan Africa.”

	Dia and Harawe will deliver a masterclass at this year’s Open Doors.

	Screening at Open Doors and a Mozambique-South Africa-Qatar, “The Prophet” begins with evangelical Pastor Hélder preaching in the village of Manjacaze. His inspiration and congregation dwindling, he turns to black magic to fire up his oratory and heal his parishioners, but his powers come at ever larger sacrifice, literally.
	

	Pointedly framed, even in vertical box aspect, bringing sense and sensitivity to shots, “The Prophet” builds as a black and white film parable about overweening ambition, becoming as well “an expression of the community [Manjacaze] that inspired it,” Luque told Variety. “The Prophet” also marked out Luque as a director to track.

	“Distributing African films, for us, means accepting a challenge that is not only operational but also theoretical and positional. Luminalia was founded precisely on this idea: to question our own ethnocentrism and bring a more conscious approach while working with non-Western titles,” Priante told Variety. 

	He added: ”We’re very happy to see that around 50% of this year’s line-up consists of African titles. This was our goal from the moment we launched the company last year, and it’s rewarding to see that established directors understand our approach, which seeks to question ethnocentrism and promote a form of distribution that involved a more theoretical and anthropological framework, not just a business model.”

schema.headline: Locarno Open Doors Buzz Title ‘Chapa 100,’ From Ique Langa, Adds Luminalia, Mo Harare, Mostafa El Kasha (EXCLUSIVE)

title: ‘The Last House’ Review: Wagner Moura and Greta Lee Bring Conviction to a Suitably Stifling Stay-at-Home Thriller
description: A decade or so ago, the premise of apocalyptic thriller “The Last House” might have sounded a little more out there than it does now: A middle-class
body:
A decade or so ago, the premise of apocalyptic thriller “The Last House” might have sounded a little more out there than it does now: A middle-class Seattle family wakes up one morning to find themselves sealed inside their house with no means of escape, a mysterious enforced house arrest that turns out to be indefinite. Post-Covid, of course, this instead plays as a fantastical spin on an experience still fresh in everyone’s minds — a familiarity that Louis Leterrier‘s film, all too aptly premiering on Netflix, uses to its claustrophobic advantage. The lockdown imposed on these four people and their immediate neighbors — and who knows how many others — may be of a more extreme and uncanny variety than the mandate that kept most of us home in 2020, but this high-concept chamber piece returns viewers to that mindset of protective panic and uncertainty. 
	

	The hows and whys of “The Last House” take it into science-fiction territory — lightly and allusively so at first, but eventually with more concrete, effects-heavy world-building (and unbuilding). But the film is most compelling throughout as a straightforward domestic drama, with increasingly fraught family dynamics lending proceedings a baseline of credibility even as whatever’s happening outside the house remains largely inscrutable. Grounded, empathetic performances by Wagner Moura and Greta Lee, as parents hanging onto their adult authority by a thread, deserve much of the credit for that, as does the intricately detailed, changeable design and conception of the house that, in a short time, becomes the characters’ entire world. 
	

	“The Last House” mostly works as a tensely enjoyable ride for times of environmental anxiety, though whether there’s any substantial meaning or resonance to the what-if scenario devised by screenwriter Matthew Robinson (“Good Luck, Have Fun, Don’t Die”) is open to question. The film touches on ideas of climate change and ecosystemic adaptation, as well as to both the virtues and limitations of community spirit, but they’re not very deeply or provocatively probed — settling for loose platitudes doled out by an unidentified female narrator. “We lived closer to each other then,” she says at the outset, describing the world before the great shut-in. “But it was easy to feel alone.”

	Not that there’s much room for loneliness in the close-knit Delgado family, who are introduced making early Christmas plans as winter sets in: They live comfortably, even if engineer dad Jason (Moura) is currently out of work, and happily, even if pre-teen siblings Graham (Noah Alexander Sosnowski) and Ruth (Riley Chung) squabble on the regular. Mom Ann (Lee) frets about signs of structural damage in their roomy midcentury home, but overall, they have it better than most — especially when, with a heavy November rainstorm raging outside, they find they literally can’t leave the house. Doors and windows are rendered unopenable by some outside force; attempts to break the glass prove likewise futile. 

	Others in their street, they discover, are similarly trapped; with the internet down and phone signals cut, they can only guess at how widespread the crisis is. At least early on, a spirit of plucky resilience prevails: Neighbors communicate by signboards, food is lightly rationed, and family movie nights alternate the only two DVDs in the house. (“Annie” and “Air Force One,” hilariously.) But as days turn to weeks, and a spartan Christmas gives way to a very unhappy new year, the family must consider the possibility that this is a grim new normal.

	If Robinson’s script is fuzzy on the logistics of who or what is keeping them inside — the explanation, when it does arrive, doesn’t exactly hold water, though Leterrier builds up to the reveal with eerie flashes of life outside the living-room window — it’s stronger on the tensions playing out indoors. As the situation grows increasingly dire, Jason and Ann are caught between their gentler duties as parents and more harshly pragmatic survival instincts; Graham and Ruth, both characters drawn, cast and played with unusual nuance, must grow up fast without any wider society to show them the way. Notwithstanding the absurdly particular conditions of its drama, “The Last House” should resonate with anyone attempting to raise children in a world physically changing before our eyes — if it raises some glum existential questions, at least Jason’s ingenious MacGyver-style apocalypse hacks offer comparative light relief.
	

	A French genre journeyman whose credits range from “The Incredible Hulk” to “Fast X,” Leterrier keeps it all ticking with the requisite balance of itchy cabin-fever atmospherics and more expansive action setpieces — though given its sometimes chintzy digital effects, the film is most effective when it plays on what you cannot see. Kevin Jenkins’ production design is the most consistent technical asset here, attentive to the detailed wear and tear of the Delgados’ moldering house as it literally cracks under pressure, as well as the ways in which it’s modified to protect and sustain its inhabitants. But there’s still everyday mess and clutter in evidence, at every stage of its evolution: “The Last House” may be silly in some respects, but it has a stabilizing sense of how life actually goes on when everything ends.

schema.headline: ‘The Last House’ Review: Wagner Moura and Greta Lee Bring Conviction to a Suitably Stifling Stay-at-Home Thriller

title: ‘The Big Bang Theory’ Star Melissa Rauch on Her Larger-Than-Life Surprise Role on ‘Stuart Fails to Save the Universe’
description:
SPOILER ALERT: This story contains spoilers from “Stuart Fails to Save the Universe” Season 1 Episode 3, now streaming on HBO Max.

	Things get witc
body:
SPOILER ALERT: This story contains spoilers from “Stuart Fails to Save the Universe” Season 1 Episode 3, now streaming on HBO Max.

	Things get witchy in Episode 3 of “Stuart Fails to Save the Universe,” and a scary, 60-foot Bernadette (Melissa Raush) makes a guest appearance. 

	The aptly titled episode, “Spoiler: Bert Is Magic,” kicks off with Bert (Brian Posehn) tied at the stake and about to be burned alive. Then he begs for it to rain — and it does. That’s the first sign that in this universe, Bert really is a wizard with magical powers. He can turn regular Coke into Diet Coke at the flick of a wrist, and hocus pocus up a cute puppy.
	

	Back in the comic book store (in this case, it’s called “The Wizard’s Sleeve” and more like a store filled with powerful, spellbinding books), Stuart (Kevin Sussman) tries to explain to the Denise (Lauren Lapkus) from last week’s universe what is exactly going on with the machine that’s transporting them across the multiverse. 


	Kripke (John Ross Bowie), who had seen Bert on the stake, makes his way back to the store. “Stuart, we have to leave here. The people in this world think science is evil.” Cracks Stuart: “How’s that different from our world?”

	Because this universe doesn’t obey the laws of physics, Kripke realizes they need magic to make the teleportation machine work. They ask Alexa where they can find someone to help — and up pops a little demon named, of course, “Alexa” (played by Louis Mustillo). Alexa points them to Bernadette Rostenkowski, “master sorceress.” 

	At first, it seems like normal Bernadette from “The Big Bang Theory.” She says she’s out of business, because the “Wizards Guild of America claimed I used my powers while we were on strike.” She tells them about a reversal spell that could get her powers back — but she needs the “blood of an innocent.” Having had just one girlfriend, Stuart works.
	

	Bert is back at the store, and turns Kripke into a penguin as revenge for leaving him at the stake. But then they’re interrupted by Wil Wheaton, who’s a wizard in this universe. He shows up to warn Stuart not to trust Bernadette. (Wheaton, of course, was frequently seen on “The Big Bang Theory” playing himself.) Turns out Bernadette is actually a demon. Bert and Wil get into a sorcery battle — and Bert wins. At the same time, Bernadette makes her potion and turns into a 60-foot monster, destroying Pasadena. She wants to rule the universe and take the machine — but Bert, with his powers, manages to get the four of them out just in time.

	“I remember a while ago getting a call from Chuck [Lorre] and he shared what the premise was, and I remember him saying that ‘you would be Bernadette, but not really, just a different version of Bernadette. So it’d be extremely different from anything you ever played.’ ” Rauch tells Variety. “And then he told me the cast, and I was just absolutely ecstatic. Because I love Kevin and Lauren and Brian and John so much, both as human beings and also just fans of theirs as actors. I think each of them is just a comedic laser in their own right.”

	In reprising Bernadette with a twist, Rauch says, “it was just so wonderful to not only be able to step back into Bernadette’s sensible loafers and her glasses, but then to be able to have this new layer to Bernadette. It sort of made some sense in this alternate universe. There’s always been this edge to Bernadette. So the fact that they then cranked that up a million notches, and now she’s also a demon, just tickled me. 

	“I just thought it was so fun to play,” she adds. “And my gosh, the fact that I get to play 80 feet tall when I’ve barely reached five feet in real life, is very thrilling. I’ve never done that sort of motion capture before. Just the scale of everything that they did there is truly extraordinary. They built an entire miniature city of Pasadena that I was able to walk through and crush and pick up little versions of people and yell at them. It was a blast.”

	Rauch says she wore a motion capture suit for the scene and “got a real high from it. Now I feel like I just want to walk around and crush things. I felt very powerful!”

schema.headline: ‘The Big Bang Theory’ Star Melissa Rauch on Her Larger-Than-Life Surprise Role on ‘Stuart Fails to Save the Universe’

title: ‘The Traitors’ India Season 2 Unveils Trailer With Karan Johar and 21-Celebrity Cast (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Prime Video India has unveiled the trailer for the second season of “The Traitors,” the unscripted celebrity competition series hosted by Karan Joha
body:
Prime Video India has unveiled the trailer for the second season of “The Traitors,” the unscripted celebrity competition series hosted by Karan Johar, set to debut exclusively on the platform on Aug. 13. New episodes will drop every Thursday.

	Filmed against the backdrop of Suryagarh Palace in Jaisalmer, Season 2 features 21 celebrity contestants drawn from across entertainment, music, and digital media: Aaditya Kulshreshth (Kullu), Abhishek Malhan (Fukraa Insaan), Ansh Chopra, Dalip Tahil, Harman Singha, Ikka Singh, Karan Singh Magic, Krystle D’souza, Mallika Sherawat, Munawar Faruqui, Parul Gulati, Prish, Ranveer Brar, Rhea Chakraborty, Rida Tharana, Sahil Salathia, Shahneel Gill, Shalini Passi, Shweta Tiwari, Soundous Moufakir and Tanya Puri. Johar is joined this season by a new character, Boo, billed as the harbinger of the “Buri Khabar” (bad news). 
	

	The show follows the established format: a group of Innocents must identify hidden Traitors before being eliminated, while the Traitors work to stay concealed and pick off their opponents. 


	Johar said: “Season 1 of ‘The Traitors’ broke through the clutter and formulaic reality content, and the audience response proved they were ready for something fresh. With Season 2, we knew we had to return with a game that was bigger, sharper, and even more unpredictable. But this time, the Players entered the palace fully aware of the format’s twists and traps, armed with strategies, stronger instincts, and a ruthlessness that caught me off guard. This season, you’ll witness friendships unravel, trust give way to paranoia, alliances crumble, and Players make choices that genuinely surprised and at times, even shocked me. That’s the beauty of ‘The Traitors’ – just when you think you’ve figured it out, the game turns everything on its head. As the host, I’ve had a front-row seat to some truly unbelievable moments, and I can honestly say I wasn’t prepared for what unfolded this season.”
	

	The trailer launch follows a promotional event in which Prime Video unveiled the full contestant lineup through a “Dining Theater of Treachery” experience. The series is produced by Dharmatic Entertainment – the digital content arm of Dharma Productions – in association with All3Media International, a global distributor that handles the format’s rights across more than 30 territories. The format, developed by IDTV, has won both BAFTA and Emmy Awards.

title: ‘La Koreana,’ a Banner New Talent Title From Spain, Brought to Market at Locarno by Producers Lazona Zinema and Estibaliz Urresola’s Sirimiri (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Sirimiri Films, founded by Estibaliz Urresola, director of Berlinale winner “20,000 Species of Bees,” is teaming with Lazona Zinema, the Basque divi
body:
Sirimiri Films, founded by Estibaliz Urresola, director of Berlinale winner “20,000 Species of Bees,” is teaming with Lazona Zinema, the Basque division of Lazona (“Spanish Affair,” “Gigantes,” “No Rest for the Wicked”) to produce “La Koreana,” one of Spain’s banner new talent titles.

	The projected feature debut of Basque writer-director Joana Moya, “La Koreana” leapt to notice last September at San Sebastián when it won the Sideral Ikusmira Berriak Prize, the top plaudit at one of Spain’s foremost development labs where Moya attended its 2025 residency. 
	

	“La Koreana” will now be brought to market at the Locarno Festival’s Match Me!, a large co-production and networking meet running Aug. 7-9 which will feature Lazona Zinema’s Jesús Choya among its producers lineup. 


	Put through Noka Ekoizpena, a San Sebastian-based women-focused mentorship and production acceleration program, “La Koreana” is set across three timelines, one in 1890 and another around 1960, set at a gigantic iron mine mountain running for miles in La Arboleda, in the Basque province of Bizkaia. 

	In 1890, the miners seem trapped in time. Around 1960, Manuela, “La Koreana,” arrives at the mine from her native Andalusia to join her husband. But the mine is already in ruins.

	The film’s synopsis begins with an image: “A mountain lurks behind the fog while hundreds of miners extract iron from within. Hypnotized by its magnetism, they will be lost in its time and its memory.” 

	The film’s “true main character,” Mora told Variety, is the mountain, “a territory on which the story of those who have worked and lived on it is written.” All the characters, human and non-human, are submitted to a process of extraction and exploitation,” Mora explained while still at Ikusmira Berriak. 
	

	“‘La Koreana’ is a film about memory and the transformation of bodies and landscapes. It’s based on a simple question: What remains in a place after it has been exploited to its limits?” she commented to Variety.

	The feature is inspired by the memories and stories of Moya’s grandmother, who made Manuela’s journey from Málaga to La Arboleda at around the same time.   

	“I wanted to produce ‘La Koreana’ because I noticed in Joana Moya’s vision a deeply personal way of engaging with our region,” Urresola told Variety. 

	“Her ability to revisit our mining past from an intimate, auteurist perspective, giving a voice to the mountain, resonates with my desire to promote a form of cinema capable of transforming the memory of the landscape into a vivid cinematic experience,” added Urresola, whose “20,000 Species of Bees,” winner of  Berlin’s best leading performance award for Sofía Otero in 2023, has the same resonant sense of place, while also raising far broader issues.

	“‘La Koreana’ is one of the most conceptually daring projects we have found and perfectly reflects our goals in this new chapter of Lazona Zinema: to support radical voices with deep roots in the Basque Country and projects capable of captivating the international auteur scene,” added Choya, who served as a delegate producer on “Sundays” and Cannes hit “Sleepless City” when working for Marisa Fernández Armenteros’ Buenapinta Media.

	Choya was one of Variety’s 2024 10 Emerging Producers to Watch selection. He now heads up Lazona Cinema, founded in Bizkaia capital Bilbao in 2024 to produce bold, risk-taking projects from emerging Basque voices and large-scale productions and international co-productions. 

	An early production, comedy “Sin Cobertura,“ scored €2.9 million ($3.4 million) at the Spanish box office last year. It has just released “A Sucker’s Born Every Minute,” Arantxa Echeverría’s follow up to smash hit “Undercover.”

title: Aymar Esse, Director of Locarno Open Doors World Premiere ‘My Father’s Kora,’ Explores the Challenges of Queer Identity in Senegal
description: “My Father’s Kora” (“La Kora de Mon Père”), a Benin-Switzerland-Germany production, will have its world premiere Aug. 9 at the Locarno Film Festival
body:
“My Father’s Kora” (“La Kora de Mon Père”), a Benin-Switzerland-Germany production, will have its world premiere Aug. 9 at the Locarno Film Festival‘s Open Doors section, which has focused on 42 countries of the African continent since 2025.

	The film follows Souleymane Everston Adowo Freudenreich, an Afro-German trans man who travels to Dakar, Senegal, to repair his father’s kora. Classified as a harp or lute, fixing the kora serves as a metaphor for Souleymane’s search for identity, belonging and acceptance within a traditional Muslim culture.
	

	“It’s a film about repair, memory, and transmission. The film listens as much as it observes, using a poetic and sensory language to explore identity, silence, faith, and the healing power of music, sewing, and the ocean. It is a quiet reflection on what can be repaired, and what remains uncertain,” says Beninese director Aymar Esse.


	“It is not an activist film in the strict sense. It is an invitation to see the other without rushing to define them, to recognize a human being before a category, and to understand that cinema can sometimes open a small breach in the wall of certainties,” he adds.

	Produced through Esse’s SunRise Films and co-produced by Aline Bonvin Film Video (Switzerland), Seera Films (Germany) and 274 Studio (Switzerland), the film was developed within the framework of Steps’ Generation Africa program, with the financial support of the Swiss Cooperation Office in Benin. It will have its German premiere at the Afrika Film Festival Köln in September.



	

									Ayéman Aymar Esse
	



	Variety interviewed Esse before the film’s world premiere.
	

	Can you tell us a little bit more about the kora?

	Aymar Esse: The kora is, for me, a profoundly living instrument, almost a voice in its own right. Born in the Mandingue cultural world, it carries a long history of transmission, memory, and poetry, and it is deeply connected to the griots, those guardians of speech, genealogy, and storytelling. In their hands, the kora is not only a musical instrument, it becomes a link between generations, between the living and the ancestors, between the past and the present. I have always been moved by its sound, something very soothing, very enveloping, almost like water flowing.

	Why did you decide to use the kora as a metaphor for Souleymane’s journey to Senegal?

	Esse: The idea of using the kora as a metaphor came from the fact that we have a musical instrument that is broken and a character who is also trying to understand himself and find where he belongs.

	Bringing the kora back to Senegal made sense to me. There, it could find original replacement parts, a new skin, which I like to think of in relation to skin color, an old calabash perhaps replaced by a new one, and new strings. For me, each part of the kora carries a meaning: the skin speaks to the body, the strings suggest a connection to Senegal, and the neck feels to me like the backbone.

	 What is the cultural view on LGBTQ issues in Senegal?

	Esse: Senegal remains a very conservative country when it comes to homosexuality, and in recent years the legal and social climate has become even harsher toward LGBTQ people. So the warmth and acceptance shown in the film should not be read as the rule, but as the fragile light of a singular family story.

	For me, Souleymane comes first as a person, as a full human being, before any label. In the film, what matters is not to reduce him to his trans identity, but to observe how he is received with unconditional love. At that point, his identity no longer weighs in the balance in the same way, because love has already made its choice. Can you talk about the ballroom scene as a safe space for the LGBTQ community?

	Esse: I did not know ballroom culture myself; it was a discovery for me. I realized how deeply people can speak to one another there, how they can breathe together in a space that becomes almost a language of its own. But beyond the ballroom itself, what stayed with me was another question. What is a safe space, really? Who creates it? Who protects it? And how do we find it in a world that often feels unsafe?
	

	Today, aren’t we all searching for some kind of shelter? From violence, from political pressure, from climate change, from loneliness, from the simple difficulty of being alive? And yet, maybe a safe space is not only something we are given. Maybe it is something we create, quietly, through trust, through shared language, through the people who see us and let us be.

title: Locarno’s Alliance 4 Development Welcomes Queer Musical, Eco Body Horror and Bruce LaBruce’s Melodrama With Monica Bellucci and Béatrice Dalle
description: Alliance 4 Development, Locarno’s co-development platform for film projects from Austria, France, Germany and Switzerland, has presented this year’s
body:
Alliance 4 Development, Locarno’s co-development platform for film projects from Austria, France, Germany and Switzerland, has presented this year’s projects. 

	The line-up includes Bruce LaBruce’s first French-led feature, “Third Take.” It’s a “female melodrama” starring Monica Bellucci and Béatrice Dalle as two actresses who reunite for a film shoot destined to “become the epiphany of their decaying romance,” he stated. 
	

	Love will also be at the heart of “Cuore Matto,” a “queer and feminist coming-of-age musical” in which director Tamer Ruggli follows a mother and a son. 


	“It explores questions of identity, freedom and social norms through a vibrant, romantic musical film,” he told Variety. 

	“Set in the late 1960s, the story unfolds during a period of profound social transformation, driven by a spirit of emancipation and the questioning of conservative values, we well as a desire to redefine social, romantic and family relationships. This era of openness and newly won freedoms strongly resonates with the present day, which is increasingly marked by identity tensions, inward-looking movements and the resurgence of reactionary rhetoric.” 

	This contrast gives the film a “distinctly contemporary relevance,” he stated. 

	“We believe the musical format is particularly well suited to this story, enabling it to reach a broad audience without compromising its artistic ambition. Music enables the characters to express emotions that words alone cannot convey, and allows the film to transcend linguistic and cultural boundaries.”
	

	Complicated family dynamics also drive Henning Beckhoff’s “Dyspnoe.” It’s a father-daughter story about “exhaustion, masculinity and the desire to escape.” 

	“Set during a three-week rehabilitation retreat on the North Sea, the film combines the intimate realism of everyday family life with the poetic transformation of a man who increasingly feels more at home underwater than on land. At its emotional core is a love story between a father and his daughter, told with tenderness, humor and a subtle sense of the fantastic,” he said. 

	In Antonio Donato’s “Shooting Watermelons,” an authoritarian father takes his two sons on a summer holiday without their mother for the first time. According to Donato, the film sets out to “peel back the layers of power that men are expected to display each day.” 

	“I return to the summer world of my youth, a place fueled by rivalry, constant comparison, and the relentless pursuit of image. My own experiences become a mirror for a larger social pattern. This film is both a journey through my memory and an act of transformation, turning private scars into a universal narrative that questions – with irony and heart – old ideas of masculinity and patriarchy.”

	Producer Santiago Fondevila Sancet added: “We were interested in this debut feature for its distinctive approach to male vulnerability, revealing it through the quiet rituals, social performances and small everyday gestures that often hide it in plain sight.” 

	He praised its “singular cinematic language, balancing awkwardness, empathy and understated humor to create an emotionally rich and deeply moving drama.” 

	“We believe the film has strong potential for European co-productions, thanks to the universal resonance of its story and the filmmaker’s growing international recognition, most recently marked by the selection of their short film ‘Oh Boys’ for Cannes’ Directors’ Fortnight.”

	Jessica Puppo’s “Reign of Silures” is set in a thermal palace on Lake Geneva, where two sisters try to survive. Producer Alexis Perrin called the film “an ecological body horror with an intimate heart.” 

	“[There are] two sisters, a dying lake and a luxury palace that devours those who serve it. Jessica transforms the betrayal of a generation taught that work would protect them into visceral cinema, where illness cracks the skin while luxury masks collapse. It combines bold world-building with a deeply emotional central relationship, making it a singular and ambitious debut feature,” he noted.
	

	Other interesting female leads can be found in “Wrecking Ball” by Clara Stern, in which a woman refuses to give up in the face of real estate issues and a crumbling marriage, and Claudia Rorarius’ sci-fi film “Humanoid” about an artist who creates an android after her partner’s death.

	“It’s an intimate drama about love, grief and the moment when artificial intelligence begins to enter our emotional lives. Through the perspective of a 48-year-old female artist, the film explores questions of identity, memory and human connection in a rapidly changing world,” she explained. 

	“With a strong female protagonist rarely represented on screen at this age, the project combines a deeply personal story with a globally relevant theme.”

	In “Magnetic Storms” by Wendy Pillonel, a young rugby talent becomes stranded in an Italian village with her mother. She contacts her father, but his arrival doesn’t help. Florian Hoffmann’s “Yazz” sees its teenage protagonist “caught between barbed wire, privilege and danger.”

	“We want to reveal a world that everyone recognizes, yet hardly anyone truly knows: life inside UN camps. Blending intimate drama with urgent political relevance, the film explores generational conflict, responsibility and the search for meaningful action in times of crisis. ‘Yazz’ is a timely arthouse film with strong international resonance and broad discussion potential,” said producer Katrin Renz. 

	“Yumi” – directed by Silvia Luzi and Luca Bellino – focuses on a girl who is constantly monitored through by her father, Gianni, through a parental control app.

	“We wanted to explore a time in which looking has replaced seeing. We scroll through images, wars, bodies and lives, believing that exposure alone is enough to make them intelligible,” they stated. “Gianni looks in the same way: his daughter’s life passes before his eyes as something to consume, and this is precisely why it eludes him.”

	“Stone Over Stone,” a new film by Hilal Baydarov, known for “Sermon to the Fish” and “In Between Dying,” will also be featured.

	“It’s about people living on the edge of visibility and about what remains after violence: silence, displacement, shame and the fragile attempt to continue living,” he said.  
	

	“Set within an unfinished high-rise in a divided Eastern European city, it follows characters who are trying to build a future while carrying the invisible ruins of war.”



	

					‘Yazz’
									Courtesy of Tellfilm
	



	A closer look at selected projects:

	“Cuore Matto”

	Switzerland

	Director: Tamer Ruggli

	Produced by Francine Lusser and Gérard Monier (Tipimages Productions), it also has Alessandra Moresco (Bliss Production) on board as an associate producer. The story, written by Ruggli and Joanne Giger, is set in 1969. Matteo, who’s 17, dreams of becoming an actor and escaping his father – as well as their grey industrial town. Sent to Ticino for the harvest, he discovers a vibrant, sensual world with Lucio and Alba. At home, his mother Giusi – trapped in an oppressive marriage – begins her own quiet emancipation. 

	“Dyspnoe”

	Germany

	Director: Henning Beckhoff

	This film, produced by Frauke Kolbmüller for Oma Inge Film, was also written by Beckhoff. It focuses on marine biologist Ludwig who’s burnt out and adrift. He takes his daughter Carlotta to a parent-child clinic on an island. Amidst therapies, shifting loyalties and the unspoken truth of an impending separation, father and daughter find themselves drawn closer together. As Ludwig’s body begins to change in unsettling ways, the cure becomes a journey through fear, loss and transformation.  

	“Humanoid”

	Germany

	Director: Claudia Rorarius

	Rorarius directs and produces this sci-fi film for Soquietfilms. Her second feature, “Touched,” premiered at Locarno and was awarded for acting. Set in the near future, it follows Elsa, who must deal with her grief following the death of her partner. She ends up creating an android in his image. What starts as an art project becomes a journey of self-empowerment. More determined than ever, Elsa challenges patriarchal structures and carves out a path for her independent motherhood.

	“Magnetic Storms”

	Switzerland

	Director: Wendy Pillonel

	Produced by Flavia Zanon for Close Up Films, the film is about Jo, a brash young rugby talent who finds herself stranded in an Italian village with her mother and without a phone, where the ground is shaking. Angry and obsessed with returning to Switzerland, she secretly contacts her father, convinced he’ll help her. But his arrival disrupts the fragile balance she thought she could control. Jo realizes she can no longer protect the silence surrounding her father’s behavior. As the ground and her world gradually crumble around her, she chooses to break free. 
	

	“Reign of Silures”

	France

	Director: Jessica Puppo

	In her feature debut, Puppo teams up with co-writer Marine Flores-Ruimi and Rumble Fish Productions. The company was founded by Alexis Perrin (formerly of Logical Pictures) and is also behind “Vesper,” “Saloum,” “Cities of Last Things” as well as the upcoming “Goliath” by Lorcan Finnegan (“Vivarium,” “The Surfer”). In the film, Maïa is a concierge at a thermal palace on Lake Geneva, where giant catfish are burned as scapegoats for a plague that cracks human skin like parched earth. When her teenage sister is placed in her care, the hotel seals itself off as a gilded fortress against the dying world. 

	“Shooting Watermelons”

	Italy

	Director: Antonio Donato

	Written by Paolo Carbone and Antonio Donato, and adapted from a short film of the same name, it’s produced by Santiago Fondevila Sancet for Cinedora – also behind “Vermiglio,” upcoming “1913” with Valeria Golino and “Klimt” by Maura Delpero. In the film, during a difficult separation, a father takes his two sons on a summer vacation. As they try to survive without their mother, the gap between them grows, especially when a wealthy foreign family arrives, sparking feelings of envy and rivalry. When a storm forces them to stay indoors, old wounds and hidden fears come to the surface, exposing their struggle to connect. 

	“Stone Over Stone”

	Austria, Poland

	Director: Hilal Baydarov

	Hilal Baydarov’s new film will show pregnant Shams and her husband Davud, who settle in an unfinished high-rise, where he works to repay gambling debts. As Davud is drawn back into addiction, Shams grows increasingly isolated among the building’s workers, veterans and outcasts. When gambling, political despair and buried violence converge, the tower’s fragile community begins to crumble. It’s produced by Georg Tiller and Maéva Ranaïvojaona for Subobscura Films (Austria) and by Korek Bojanowski for AsterFilm (Poland).

	“Third Take”

	France

	Director: Bruce LaBruce

	Award-winning artist Bruce LaBruce returns with another film. Set in a not-so-distant future, “Thrid Take” is about two actresses who were once in love and reunite in a villa for a film shoot. “It’s a hyper-referential ‘meta film’ exploring the essence of being an actress,” stated LaBruce, noting that this “female melodrama blends classical glamour with raw realism. The idea is to synthesize cinematic obsessions and diverse visual formats to create an explosive work about human resilience and the profound strength of women.” Nicolas Brevière (Local Films) produces, while Monica Bellucci and Béatrice Dalle will star. 
	

	“Wrecking Ball”

	Austria

	Director: Clara Stern

	With Michael Kitzberger producing for Nikolaus Geyrhalter Filmproduktion, Stern follows “Breaking the Ice” with a story about Eva, who – as it was stated – “runs up and down the dusty stairs in a bright yellow raincoat, exposing the real estate investor’s schemes, rallying her neighbors and fighting with her husband, wondering what went wrong.” Her protagonist is “fueled by frantic hope, love and humor. And a deep, buried anger.” Stern compared the film to a “pressure cooker.” “It combines two topics that make me angry: the real estate’s gambling with people’s homes paired with inequality in relationships.”

	“Yazz” 

	Switzerland, Germany, France

	Director: Florian Hoffmann

	Hoffmann’s film is produced by Katrin Renz for Zurich-based Tellfilm, Nicole Gerhards for Niko Films and Xénia Maingot for France’s Eaux Vives Productions. It will be shot in Switzerland and France, and tells the story of Yazz: a teenager who grows up on a UN compound in the Central African Republic. A secret escape to see her local boyfriend, Joseph, ends in an accident that tears her family apart. Ten years later, her mother reappears in Switzerland – with Joseph by her side. Forced to face her first love and her own guilt, Yazz must consider whether old wounds can truly heal or only leave scars.

	“Yumi”

	Italy

	Directors: Silvia Luzi, Luca Bellino

	This Stemal Entertainment and Bokeh Film production was overseen by Donatella Palermo, who has worked with the Taviani brothers, Ermanno Olmi and Gianfranco Rosi. The film’s protagonist, Yumi, is 13 and searching for her place in the world. Gianni, her father, monitors her through a parental control app, convinced he is protecting her – until that ordinary device becomes his own private cinema: vertical, unsettling and intimate. When Yumi begins to feel watched, she reacts by defying the lens, turning being 13 into a ruthless performance until an invisible threshold is crossed.

title: OnlyFans Model Maeurn Using Profits to Build School in the Philippines
description:
OnlyFans Star Maeurn Smiles
                          Trading Paywall for School Hall!!!
body:
OnlyFans Star Maeurn Smiles
                          Trading Paywall for School Hall!!!
                      
      
    
            OnlyFans model Maeurn Smiles is taking her success from the paywall to the school hall ... building a school and learning center in the Philippines with her OF profits.
      
    
            Maeurn tells TMZ ... she always had her sights set on teaching, but her family couldn't swing college. Still, she got a taste of the classroom ... teaching English to Chinese students before the internet took her career in a very different direction.
      
    
            Now she's bringing that dream full circle ... buying land in Cebu for 1.75 million pesos in 2024 to build a school.
      

            The big school isn't finished yet ... but Maeurn opened a smaller learning center in 2025, where local kids can do science experiments, cooking activities, and other hands-on learning.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Maeurn says she originally planned to donate the land and let the government build the school ... but when she learned that meant she couldn't name it after her father, she decided to take on the construction herself.
      
    
            Forget going back to school ... Maeurn's building one!

description:

body:
Toni Braxton
                          Resolves 6-Figure Tax Debt ...
                          Years After Bankruptcy Battle
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 7, 2026
                            1:00 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Toni Braxton says she dropped some serious dough to settle a debt with the IRS … over a decade after she finalized her second bankruptcy.
      
    
            According to official records, the singer was hit with a federal tax lien on June 22 ... and Uncle Sam said she owed A LOT of money.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The breakdown of the debt is $69,390 for 2022, $278,876 for 2023, and $250,358 for 2024 ... totaling around $598K.
      
    
            A rep for Toni tells TMZ the singer paid off the bill.  
      

            As TMZ previously reported, the "Braxton Family Values" star filed for bankruptcy in 1998 after a battle over money with her record label.
      
    
            The singer was criticized heavily for her debt … and was even scolded by Oprah during an episode of her talk show. 
      
    
            Toni's money problems arose again in 2010, when she filed for bankruptcy a second time, claiming she owed millions to creditors. 
      
    
            The second bankruptcy was closed in 2015.

body:
Sydney Sweeney & Scooter Braun
                          From Hollywood to Helping Out ...
                          New Pics Show Spokane Relief Work
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 6, 2026
                            5:15 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Sydney Sweeney and Scooter Braun continue rolling up their sleeves to help wildfire victims in her Washington hometown ... packing and organizing donations at a local food bank.
      
    
            TMZ obtained new photos of Sydney and Scooter volunteering at Second Harvest Food Bank in Spokane, where they worked alongside other volunteers to sort and prepare donations for families impacted by the devastating fires.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The couple also took photos with volunteers ... and we're told their presence helped lift everyone’s spirits during an incredibly difficult time for the community.
      

            Their hands-on effort comes as Sydney’s partnership with American Eagle expands into wildfire relief. As TMZ first reported, customers can donate to relief efforts while shopping online or in stores by rounding up their purchase total or contributing an amount of their choosing from August 7 to 31.
      
    
            The money raised will go directly to Second Harvest.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            As we reported, Sydney and Scooter have remained boots on the ground in the Spokane area, bringing food to firefighters, preparing and distributing meals and helping displaced families secure food and shelter. They’ve also volunteered with World Central Kitchen, while Sydney has made major donations to several relief organizations.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The disaster hits especially close to home for the “Euphoria” star, who grew up in Spokane and still has family in the area. Sydney recently revealed the wildfires have directly affected members of her own family.
      
    
            The Spokane-area fires have scorched more than 10,000 acres, destroyed hundreds of structures and forced tens of thousands of residents from their homes.

body:
Nolan Wells Family Lawyer
                          Ben Crump Says Don't Let Trump's Attorney Distract You!!!
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 6, 2026
                            5:00 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            Ben Crump isn't sweating Nolan Wells' friends turning to Trump's lawyer for help.
      
    
            We caught up with the prominent civil rights attorney in NYC Thursday ... and he says the boys' choice of attorney is just a distraction.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Crump tells us the only thing that matters to him and Nolan's family is getting to the truth about what happened.
      

            As we previously reported, Warren Hudson, Jax Pitalo and Morgan Seymour have enlisted the help of Attorney J. Tyler Cox and defamation lawyer Edward Andrew Paltzik.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Paltzik has represented DT in big battles with the media, like the ones against CBS/Paramount, The New York Times, and BBC.
      
    
            But Crump says calling in such big guns is just noise ... and finding out how Nolan died is what's really important.
      
    
            Cox and Paltzik want to know what happened too ... and they're going to Horn Island tomorrow to get a look at where Nolan disappeared and was found dead.
